study.title: Genesis 4 From the offering refused to the public worship of the LORD
study.overview: Genesis 4 shows, in sequence, how sin already present in the human heart expands from envy to murder, from the breaking of communion with God to the construction of a culture marked both by human conquests and violence. The chapter contrasts two paths within the same family: Cain, who rejects divine correction and departs from the presence of the LORD, and the lineage of Seven, in which mankind comes back to call upon the name of the LORD. The text does not present a story only about two brothers, but about the moral and spiritual division of humanity, on the gravity of sin and on the mercy of God that still preserves life and opens up space for worship.

outline.title: Birth, vocation and divine warning
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the birth of Cain and Abel, their occupations and their offerings to the Lord. God looks for at Abel and his offering, but not for Cain and his offering. The problem is revealed within Cain: anger, anger, abatement and resistance to divine warning. The LORD calls him to repentance and shows him that sin is at the door, demanding moral dominion.

outline.title: Homicide, Judgment and Curse
outline.explanation: Cain leads hostility to the extreme and kills Abel. God confronts him, exposing the guilt and listening to the cry of innocent blood. The sentence involves the land, now linked to violence, and the future of Cain, who begins to live as a wandering and fugitive, without the same fertility of the land he cultivated.

outline.title: Tension between judgment and mercy
outline.explanation: Cain recognizes the weight of his guilt and fears being killed by others. The LORD, however, limits retaliation and places a protective sign on Cain. Even without nullifying the punishment, God preserves the life of the guilty and prevents revenge from becoming even more destructive.

outline.title: The lineage of Cain and the beginning of the invocation of the LORD
outline.explanation: Cain builds a city and his offspring develops forms of urban, pastoral, musical and metallurgical life, but also deepens violence in Lameque. Then the birth of Seven opens a new genealogical line, culminating in Enos, when men begin to call upon the name of the LORD. The chapter ends with a sign of hope: despite human corruption, worship of the LORD appears again publicly.

study.context: The text presupposes a very early scenario of human history, after the fall narrated in Genesis 3. References to the altar, offering, sacrifice, and invocation of the name of the LORD indicate a religious life already existing in the human family, even though the chapter does not detail when these practices began. The chapter itself also organizes two lines: that of Cain, marked by remoteness, violence and cultural expansion, and that of Sete, associated with the worship of the LORD. The focus of the narrator is not to give a complete chronology, but to show how rebellion and faith develop in opposite paths.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God not only evaluates the external act, but also the disposition of the heart. Cain's offer is rejected in connection with his inner posture, while Abel appears as an example of accepted offer. Sin is portrayed as a real force that seeks to dominate the person but must be dominated. The murder of Abel reveals that human violence affects not only the neighbor, but also the creation, because the land carries the weight of the shed blood. Still, God acts with justice and mercy: he judges evil, protects Cain's life and preserves the continuity of human history. Finally, Genesis 4 presents true hope not in the violent lineage of Cain, but in the restoration of worship, when mankind comes back to invoke the name of the LORD.

scholarViews.insight: Enos is presented as the moment when people began to invoke the name of the LORD; the note links this invocation to the worship expressed in sacrifice and prayer, marking the beginning of a public practice of worship.

The commentator understands that, in a given time, Cain and Abel brought offers to the LORD, probably based on a religious practice already prescribed by God to the family, showing that the cult did not arise on isolated human initiative.

The note notes that the expression about Enos can be understood as the beginning of a distinction between true worshipers and others, although it also recognizes an alternative reading in which profanation would have begun.

questions: What does the text reveal about the relationship between the state of the heart and the acceptance of our worship of God?
How does God's response to Cain at the same time show justice against sin and mercy toward the sinner?
In what ways does the history of Cain's lineage and the lineage of Seven challenge the way we evaluate success, culture and piety?
study.practice: Examine your life in the light of this chapter: before asking whether your offer, service or religious participation is right, ask if your heart is submitted to the Lord. Quickly confess anger, envy and the desire to justify the error before they turn into destructive actions. He also seeks to restore the concrete practice of the invocation of the name of the LORD through regular prayer, sincere worship and daily dependence on God. Where there is conflict, choose reconciliation instead of the escalation of revenge. And remember that God can still preserve, correct and reorient a story marked by serious faults.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not explain in detail why Cain's offer was rejected, so any conclusion needs to be made with caution and without stating more than the text says. Notes cite different interpretations of what Cain's speech means at 4:8 and the 4:26 expression, including alternative readings; therefore, these issues should be addressed as interpretive possibilities, not as absolute certainty. Nor is there enough basis here to affirm historically accurately when exactly the formal sacrifice began, the invocation of the name of the LORD or the social organization described in the genealogies.
